scene.testo: They asked him a simple question. Why us? Why not the Russians, the British, or the French? In May 1945, American officers put that question to the man who built the V-2 rocket. His answer took only a few sentences.

It was Wednesday, May 2, 1945. A young German pedaled a bicycle down a mountain road near the Austrian border. He was searching for American soldiers. He had a message that would sound absurd to any sentry on duty.

He found one. In careful English, he told the American that his brother had invented the V-2 rocket and wanted to surrender. The soldier assumed the man was insane. Within days, though, the brother sat before American interrogators.

His name was Wernher von Braun. He was thirty-three years old. He had built the first long-range ballistic missile ever used in war. Now he faced a question that every German specialist was asking himself that spring.
Why surrender to the Americans? Von Braun had an answer ready. But it was not the whole truth. To understand what he said, and what he left out, we have to go back to the last days of April.
At the end of April 1945, von Braun and about a dozen of his top engineers waited out the war in a ski hotel at Oberjoch, high in the Bavarian Alps. They had not chosen to be there.

SS General Hans Kammler had moved the rocket team south from central Germany. SS guards watched them. Among the engineers, a rumor spread that the SS would rather shoot them than let them fall into enemy hands.
No such order has ever been found. But the men in that hotel believed it. They were isolated, frightened, and running out of time. Then, on May 1, the radio announced that Adolf Hitler was dead.

The guards scattered and left. The next morning, the engineers decided not to wait for anyone to find them. They sent Magnus von Braun, Wernher's younger brother, because his English was the best in the group.

The American who stopped him was Private First Class Frederick Schneikert, of the 44th Infantry Division. Schneikert passed the matter to division counterintelligence. They sent Magnus back up the mountain with instructions: bring the others with you.

That evening, a small convoy of German cars rolled down the road toward the American lines. In one of them sat the man who built the V-2, his left arm in a huge cast from a car accident weeks earlier.

At Reutte, in Austria, the rocket team gave itself up. The prisoners were not what the soldiers expected. Von Braun was tall, cheerful, and talkative. He grinned for the cameras, posed with American troops, and shook hands.

He asked for nothing except permission to keep working. One American who watched him that week said they had captured either the greatest scientist in the Third Reich, or its greatest liar. So the Americans asked him directly.

Why did you surrender to us? Von Braun did not answer with one sentence. He gave three reasons. They were not his alone. They reflected how the whole rocket team had weighed its choices in the final weeks.

Years later, one member of the group put the team's reasoning in a single line. We despise the French. We are mortally afraid of the Soviets. We do not think the British can afford us. That leaves the Americans.

Three nations were ruled out, one after another, and each had its reasons. France had been occupied by Germany for four years. The engineers could expect little goodwill there, and they said so among themselves.

The Soviet Union had lost millions of people to the German invasion. The engineers expected no mercy there. Britain had been struck by more than a thousand V-2 rockets, and it was close to bankruptcy.
Only one country still had the money, the factories, and the empty desert needed to keep building rockets. When von Braun wrote it down for his captors, he put it in more careful language.

He wrote that the choice of which victorious nation to entrust with this invention was, above all, a moral decision. He said the team wanted to spare the world another war like the one Germany had just lived through.

It was a noble explanation. But it left out one thing. The V-2 had been built underground, in tunnels dug into a mountain near Nordhausen. The factory was called the Mittelwerk. Its workers were prisoners.

They came from the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp. About sixty thousand prisoners passed through that camp, and about twenty thousand died. More people died building the V-2 than were killed by it.
Von Braun had been a member of the Nazi Party since 1937, and an officer in the SS since 1940. He had visited the tunnels. In the summer of 1944, he went to Buchenwald to select skilled prisoners.
None of this appeared in the statement he gave the Americans. But there was something else he told them. A year earlier, in March 1944, the Gestapo had arrested him in the middle of the night.

The charge was defeatism. Informers reported that he said the war was going badly, and that he cared more about spaceflight than weapons. He spent two weeks in a cell at Stettin before being released.

General Walter Dornberger and Albert Speer secured his release. To the Americans, the Gestapo story carried the meaning he wanted them to take from it. He was never merely a weapons man. And now he had to prove it.
Interrogators moved the team to Garmisch-Partenkirchen and asked von Braun to put on paper where rockets would go next. He did not write a technical summary. He wrote a vision of the future.
He described the V-2 as only a beginning. He wrote of multistage rockets, of rockets that could cross the Atlantic, of an artificial satellite circling the Earth, and of a manned station in orbit.

From there, he said, a voyage to the Moon would someday be possible. The war with Japan was still being fought. The atomic bomb had not yet been used. Yet a prisoner was describing flight to the Moon.

It was also a sales pitch. The report told the Americans what they would lose if they let this team go. And they already knew who else was looking. The Red Army reached Peenemuende, the rocket center on the Baltic coast, on May 5.

The underground plant at Nordhausen lay inside the zone that would be turned over to the Soviets in July. American officers worked fast. Before the handover, they shipped out parts for about one hundred V-2 rockets.
Major Robert Staver tracked down fourteen tons of Peenemuende documents that the engineers had hidden in a mine, and moved them out of the area days before the British took control of it.

In October 1946, the Soviets ran their own recruitment. In a single night, they put more than two thousand German specialists and their families on trains to the Soviet Union, whether the Germans wanted to go or not.

Von Braun never had to make that trip. In September 1945, he landed in the United States under a secret military program, first called Overcast and later Paperclip. By early 1946, over one hundred of his team were at Fort Bliss, Texas.

They were officially prisoners of war and could not leave the post without an escort. In April 1946, at White Sands Proving Ground in New Mexico, they began firing V-2 rockets rebuilt from parts shipped out of Nordhausen.

Twelve years later, on January 31, 1958, von Braun's team launched Explorer 1, the first American satellite. Then they built the Saturn V. On July 16, 1969, Apollo 11 rose toward the Moon, the voyage he had described at Garmisch.

descrizione:
In May 1945, American officers asked Wernher von Braun why he and his rocket team surrendered to the United States instead of the Soviets, British, or French. This documentary follows the documented story: the ski hotel in the Bavarian Alps, the bicycle ride of Magnus von Braun, the surrender at Reutte, and the three-nation reasoning behind the choice.

We also examine what von Braun left out of his statement: the Mittelwerk tunnels near Nordhausen, the Mittelbau-Dora prisoners, and the human cost of building the V-2. His Garmisch report, the race with the Red Army, and Operation Paperclip explain how a captured rocket team became the foundation of the American space program.

Watch to the end for the consequence, from Fort Bliss and White Sands to Explorer 1 and Apollo 11.
